Romeo and Juliet. The tragedy by William Shakespeare, written early in his career around 1595, depicting the doomed love of two young people from warring families in Verona, Italy. The play explores themes of fate, family hatred, sexual desire, and the destructive power of vengeance through the lovers' brief, intense passion and its tragic conclusion.

The action is set among two feuding noble families, the Montagues and the Capulets, whose hatred poisons the whole city and ultimately destroys their children. Romeo, a Montague, and Juliet, a Capulet, meet at a masked ball and fall instantly in love. They secretly marry the next day—a rebellion against family duty and ancient grudge. Friar Lawrence facilitates their marriage and devises a plan to reunite them. Juliet will drink a potion to feign death. Romeo will retrieve her from the tomb, and they will flee together. But the plan fails due to miscommunication. Romeo, believing Juliet truly dead, kills himself at her tomb. Juliet wakes to find him dead and kills herself in despair.

Themes of fate run throughout the play. The lovers are called "star-crossed," and the play explores whether their doom is written into destiny or self-inflicted through rash action. The lovers' deaths finally shame the Montagues and Capulets into ending their feud, but at the cost of two innocent lives—the play's tragic irony. Shakespeare emphasizes this through some of literature's most celebrated poetic language: sonnets, metaphors of light and darkness, passionate soliloquies that capture the intensity of youthful, all-consuming romantic love.

Romeo and Juliet examines how private emotion collides with public feuding, making it one of literature's most famous meditations on love and death. The play remains the template for how Western culture understands both doomed romance and the tragedy that stems not from moral failing but from circumstances beyond the lovers' control. In this way, it stands alongside Shakespeare's later tragedies like Hamlet and Othello, works that explore how destructive emotion can overwhelm reason, though Romeo and Juliet traces this collapse specifically through the lens of thwarted love.
